## Abstract

Environmental exposures shape disease risk, but the generalizability of circulating protein-based readouts of exposures across diverse populations remains unknown. Using plasma proteomic profiles of 5,416 proteins in 10,043 participants from the All of Us Research Program, we evaluated associations with and composite scores of 100+ exposures, spanning adiposity, air pollution, ambient temperature, and substance use. We find that proteomic exposure signatures are largely consistent across populations and socioeconomic strata, with <1% of proteins showing significant cross-population heterogeneity, which included BMI as an exception, with leptin being the most heterogeneous association. Population-specific leptin trajectories adiposity, together with residual leptin-type 2 diabetes associations after BMI adjustment, revealed sex-specific metabolic risk not captured by BMI alone. Aggregated protein scores were largely exposure-specific, but substance-use scores showed cross-prediction and SES scores were broadly associated. PM2.5 protein scores captured within-region exposure variation and outperformed geographic and socioeconomic correlates, but spatial confounders remain embedded within protein-environment associations. Scores trained in UK Biobank transferred to All of Us for biologically proximal exposures, supporting cross-biobank portability. These findings establish plasma proteomics as a scalable framework for exposure measurement across diverse populations, while underscoring that responsible applications require careful consideration of biological context, social patterning, and cohort structure.

## Introduction

Environmental exposures shape disease risk across the life course, but they are often measured inconsistently and/or subjectively across datasets, and the molecular processes they perturb remain incompletely characterized. Plasma proteomics is well positioned to inform the molecular processes that environmental exposures perturb because circulating proteins can accurately capture these and downstream physiologic responses. Recent large-scale studies have shown that modifiable lifestyle and clinical exposures, including smoking, alcohol use, dietary behavior, exercise, adiposity, renal function, and inflammation, are associated with widespread variation in the plasma proteome (1). Protein-based models of incident disease outperform traditional clinical models and polygenic risk scores for a wide range of diseases (2–4) (e.g. AUC > 0.8 for 92 diseases (5)). However, accumulating evidence suggests that many disease-associated proteins are not themselves causal drivers. Instead, a substantial fraction of their predictive signal appears to reflect environmental risk exposure, early physiologic dysregulation, or subclinical disease processes. Notably, over 90% of proteins associated with diseases like lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are also associated with smoking, and disease-associated proteins tested in Mendelian randomization analysis show smoking associations at a markedly higher rate (640 of 782, 82%) than the general background rate across all measured proteins (1,673 of 2,923, 57%) (2, 6). Thus, improving biological interpretation of disease-predictive proteomic signatures will require two complementary approaches: first, identifying proteins causally implicated in disease and defining the mechanisms through which they act; and second (the focus of this study), developing quantitative proteomic measures of environmental exposures that clarify the exposure histories and longitudinal trajectories giving rise to these signatures. Disentangling the causal from the correlative roles those exposures play in disease risk benefits from integration of genomic and environmental data and is a key step towards more precisely intervening to minimize disease risk or progression. Understanding the degree to which genetic and environmental exposures contribute to proteomic variation requires consideration at individual proteins versus across the entire proteome. At the level of individual proteins, the variance in abundance is shaped by both genetic and environmental architecture, though genetic contributions are more pervasive. Integrating genetic, exposomic, and proteomic data from the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) has revealed extensive genetic regulation, with 2,021 proteins (75% of 2,686 measured proteins) exhibiting genetic R2 values greater than 1%, compared to 926 proteins (34% of measured) influenced by exposomic factors at the same threshold (7). In addition, modifiable factors explain meaningful variation across many proteins; body composition traits, such as body mass index (BMI; median 0.36%, up to 7.99%), total fat mass (median 0.55%, up to 40.30%) or peripheral fat (median 0.26%, up to 7.23%) are among the exposures most strongly reflected in circulating protein profiles (1). However, in aggregate, proteomic patterns capture substantial non-genetic information to quantify environmental history. Prior studies have developed proteomic scores for smoking and alcohol consumption and demonstrated strong discrimination between current and never users (AUC > 0.95 and 0.98, respectively), supporting the use of plasma proteomic profiles as quantitative measures of environmental exposures (6, 8, 9). These objective measures are therefore poised more broadly for studies of environmental exposures and health disparities. A major barrier to broader research and translational use of these findings is uncertainty around the generalizability of proteomic signatures across computed genetic ancestry, race and/or ethnicity, and socioeconomic groups, as many foundational proteomic studies have been conducted in ancestrally, culturally, and socioeconomically homogeneous populations (10, 11). Leveraging the diversity of the All of Us (AoU) cohort across these strata, we sought to evaluate proteomic signatures of environmental exposures to characterize their biological and contextual relevance. ## Proteins associate with many exposures with varying specificity

After quality control of the AoU Olink HT 5k proteomic data, 9,561 samples and 5,414 proteins were retained for analysis (Fig. 1, fig. S1, table S1). We tested protein associations with 108 health-related exposure variables spanning behavioral, socioeconomic, environmental, anthropometric, clinical and biomarker domains (table S2), identifying 62,042 significant protein-exposure pairs at a Bonferroni-corrected threshold. These health-related exposures were selected to reflect domains commonly evaluated in prior social and environmental determinants of health frameworks, expanded to include additional environmental variables available through AoU's geocoded neighborhood-level data. These should not be viewed as fully environmental, however, as they each carry a heritable component (mean h2 = 0.16, range 0.10-0.28 across trait classes), indicating that even the least heritable exposure category retains a non-trivial genetic contribution, as observed in other biobanks previously (12). The proportion of significant proteins per exposure broadly followed the specificity and biological proximity of the trait, from anthropometric (adiposity) and biomarkers (each associated with roughly a third of proteins) to socioeconomic and air pollution measures (each under 10%) (Fig. 2A, table S3). About half of the measured proteins were associated with age (49.4%) and BMI (47.7%), followed by sex at birth (referred to hereafter as “sex”; see methods for details) (34.5%). Notably, 18.9% of proteins were associated with current cigarette smoking, a smaller proportion than reported in UKB (57% (6)), consistent with reduced statistical power in AoU and reflected by downsampling (Supplementary text). We first assessed whether circulating proteins capture molecular signatures of environmental variation beyond broad geographic confounding (Fig. 1). For most geocoded exposures, adjustment for region of residence (Northeast, Midwest, West, or South) substantially attenuated the number of significant protein associations (fig. S2, table S3), reducing associations by an average of 87.8% for ambient temperature, 30.5% for SES, and 15.3% for air pollution exposures—consistent with a major contribution of geographic structure to these signals. In contrast, PM2.5-associated proteins increased after regional adjustment, suggesting that regional differences masked rather than explained within-region associations. Several proteins remained associated with PM2.5 (365d avg) after regional adjustment with prior links to respiratory disease biology, including SERPINA1 (13), IL1RL1 (14), CHI3L1 (15), and IL6R (16), all inversely associated with PM2.5 (table S4). These findings suggest the PM2.5-associated proteomic signature may capture biologically relevant inflammatory and airway-related variation beyond broad regional structure, though this remains correlational rather than causal evidence of mediation. Similarly, region-adjusted associations with ambient temperature implicated proteins with prior links to heat stress and heat acclimation biology (table S4). Notably, C1QTNF1, MOG, and SMOC1 overlap with proteins previously reported in human heat-acclimation studies (17). By contrast, canonical heat-shock chaperones HSPA1A and HSPB1 (18–20), which were significantly associated with temperature before regional adjustment, became insignificant after adjustment, suggesting that regional structure explains their apparent temperature association, while a distinct subset of heat-stress-related proteins remain robust to regional confounding (Supplementary text). Second, we estimated group-stratified exposure-protein associations to test for heterogeneity across genetically inferred ancestry groups (EUR-like, AMR-like, AFR-like, EAS-like, and SAS-like) or self-reported race and/or ethnicity groups (White, Hispanic, Black, Asian, and Mixed) (Fig. 1). We focused primarily on stratifying by self-reported race and/or ethnicity, as environmental and social exposures are expected to be socially patterned, but retained genetically inferred ancestry for validating protein scores derived from ancestrystratified discovery cohorts. Notably, as ancestry is a continuum, these groupings are artificial and should not be conflated with social constructs such as race and/or ethnicity; they are used to compare with existing studies (e.g. UKB). Overall, evidence of heterogeneity was limited: across more than 100 exposures, fewer than 1% of proteins per exposure showed significant heterogeneity by Cochran's Q after Bonferroni-corrected meta-analysis, with no difference between ancestry- and race- and/or ethnicity-based stratification (median

Proteomic signatures of air pollution reflect individual exposure as well as broader geographic and environmental structure

A key question in proteomic exposure modeling is whether protein scores reflect individual-level exposure variation or instead capture geographic and socioeconomic structure correlated with exposure. We addressed this directly for PM2.5 by evaluating the spatial distribution of the PM2.5 protein score, its specificity relative to related environmental and geographical scores, and its transferability across biobanks. To evaluate spatial concordance, we summarized residential PM2.5 estimates and PM2.5 protein scores to ZIP3 regions by population-density weighting and compared tertile assignments across 247 regions with complete data (Fig. 3A). Overall concordance between observed and predicted PM2.5 was 46.6%. Some local discordance was also evident (5.7% high observed/low protein score; 4.0% low observed/high protein score ZIPs), which may reflect residual geographic or socioeconomic confounding, exposure misclassification, temporal mismatch, or individual-level heterogeneity in exposure or biological response. To assess specificity, we compared the PM2.5 protein scores against five additional protein scores — each trained in the held-out test set to predict a related environmental or geographic trait (urbanization, 365-day ambient temperature, 30-day ozone, longitude, and latitude) (Fig. 3B-C, table S12). In univariate models, the PM2.5 protein score was most strongly correlated with measured annual PM2.5 (R2 = 0.064) (table S9), with the urbanization score contributing modestly (R2= 0.015), and all protein scores were significantly associated with the PM2.5 protein score (Fig. 3C). In a joint model including all six scores, the PM2.5 score explained the largest independent fraction of PM2.5 variance (incremental partial R2 = 0.051 [0.035-0.069]), followed by a smaller contribution from the urbanization protein score (partial R2 = 0.020 [0.011-0.032]), and little additional information from temperature, ozone, longitude, and latitude scores (Fig. 3B). The full six-score model explained only modestly more variance than the PM2.5 alone (R2 = 0.053 [0.040-0.074]), indicating limited independent information from the remaining environmental and geographic scores. The higher accuracy of the PM2.5 score compared to all geographical and environmental correlates, indicates that it captures individuallevel exposure signal beyond geographical structure alone. Nevertheless, the PM2.5 score was associated with a broader set of traits beyond air pollution, including inflammatory, metabolic, hematologic, renal, and hepatic markers, as well as smoking-related and socioeconomic variables (table S9). Rather than undermining specificity, this pattern suggests that protein scores for environmental exposures inherently encode the physiological consequences of the exposure as it occurs in the population, making them biological measures of real-world exposure patterns rather than isolated biomarkers of a single measured variable. Cross-biobank transferability was limited, providing further evidence that PM2.5 protein signatures are partly geography-dependent. UKB-derived air pollution scores showed minimal predictive performance in AoU, with the strongest signal restricted to NO2 in AMR-like participants (incremental R2 = 0.050 [0.033-0.071], versus ≤0.016 in all other ancestry groups) (fig. S5, table S6). This association attenuated substantially after adjustment for geographic region (fig. S12), suggesting that it captured geographic structure rather than individual-level exposure variation alone, consistent with our within-AoU validation results. Differences in exposure definitions and temporal windows between UKB and AoU likely also contributed to this limited portability (Supplementary text).

## Proteomic exposure signatures reflect socially patterned metabolic context

## Heterogeneity in BMI-associated proteomic signatures across population strata.

We stratified exposure-protein association analyses across genetic ancestry and self-reported race and/or ethnicity groups to evaluate heterogeneity. Among all exposures examined, BMI showed the greatest degree of heterogeneity (fig. S3), with 111 (2.05%) and 116 (2.14%) proteins meeting our heterogeneity criteria (fixedeffect meta-analysis Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.05 and Cochran's Q P < 1.66 × 10-5) across ancestry and race and/or ethnicity groups, respectively. Leptin was the most heterogeneous BMI-associated protein across ancestry (Cochran Q test p-value [phet]=1.38 × 10-19) and the fifth most heterogeneous across race and/or ethnicity groups (phet=1.97 × 10-11). BMI itself is highly heterogeneous across race and/or ethnicity groups, with the lowest mean and standard deviation in self-identified Asian participants (25.6 kg/m² [4.6]) to highest in selfidentified Black participants (29.5 kg/m² [7.0]); comparable patterns were observed by computed genetic ancestry (fig. S13, table S13). This phenotypic heterogeneity extended to socioeconomic strata: BMI-protein score correlations were modestly higher in lower-SES groups (low-SES r = 0.850, low education r = 0.848;mean BMI = 29.1 kg/m² in both), than in higher-SES groups (high-income r = 0.829, high-education r = 0.824; mean BMI = 26.9 kg/m² and 26.5 kg/m², respectively). Deprivation gradients were less consistent, though correlation was still higher in the high-deprivation group (r = 0.864; mean BMI = 28.5 kg/m²) versus lowdeprivation group (r = 0.847; mean BMI = 27.3 kg/m²) (Fig. 4A, fig. S7, table S8). These patterns indicate that BMI-associated protein signatures track socioeconomic exposure gradients, in addition to the variation observed across race and/or ethnicity categories, consistent with a socially patterned component to this heterogeneity. To assess whether cross-race and/or -ethnicity differences in BMI protein score performance reflected differing BMI distributions, we repeated the analysis after matching each group's BMI distribution to that of self-identified Asian participants, who had the smallest mean BMI. BMI score correlations decreased for all groups after matching, narrowing the gap relative to the Asian reference by roughly half for self-identified Black and self-identified White participants (fig. S14, Table S14). Baseline T2D prevalence also differed by race and/or ethnicity, matching BMI distributions substantially narrowed this gap across groups, consistent with BMI as a substantial partial mediator of racial disparities in T2D prevalence. As discussed above with downsampling to match smoking status prevalence, protein score generalizability across race/ethnicity groups remains relatively high, though gaps persist that are likely attributable in part to differences in socioeconomic status. Consistent with this, numerous disparities by race/ethnicity are embedded directly in the EHR itself (fig. S15). For example, mean EHR completeness was highest among Black and White participants and markedly lower among Asian participants. Black and Hispanic participants additionally reported substantially higher rates of public versus private insurance and greater difficulty affording specialist care than White or Asian participants. The magnitude and ranking of BMI-leptin associations was sensitive to the BMI transformation applied (raw values, z scores, and inverse rank normal transformation (IRNT), underscoring the need for caution when interpreting relative effect sizes across populations (fig. S13, Supplementary text). BMI was positively associated with leptin in all race and/or ethnicity groups, with substantial heterogeneity in effect sizes (phet = 1.97 × 10-11), strongest in self-identified Black and self-identified White individuals and attenuated in selfidentified Asian participants, with comparable patterns by genetic ancestry (Fig. 4B, fig. S13). This heterogeneity was more pronounced in females than males (phet = 2.62 × 10-7 for female and 8.54 × 10-4 for male), with comparable sex-stratified patterns across race and/or ethnicity and genetic ancestry groups. We next assessed whether leptin contributes to T2D risk independently of BMI (Fig. 4E, table S15). In males, leptin was positively associated with T2D risk across all race and/or ethnicity groups prior to BMI adjustment,

## Proteomic signatures distinguish related behavioral exposures

Cigarette smoking and marijuana use were highly prevalent in the AoU proteomic cohort, with substantial heterogeneity across demographic and socioeconomic strata (fig. S17 to S21, table S16 to S17, and Supplementary text). Overall, 47.3% (3,979/8,418) of participants reported ever using marijuana and 34.8% (2,926/8,418) reported ever smoking cigarettes, with substantial co-use: 70.9% of smokers also used marijuana, while 47.9% of marijuana users also smoked cigarettes (Fig. 5A, fig. Substance use prevalence varied by age, sex, race and/or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and geography, consistent with established U.S. social patterning (22) and differences in regulatory environments (23, 24).

## Shared and distinct proteomic associations of marijuana use and cigarette smoking

At the individual protein level, marijuana use and cigarette smoking shared 190 Bonferroni-significant proteins (Fig. 5B, table S18), with the strongest tissue enrichment in the lung (-log10FDR = 7.14, OR = 6.3) (Fig. 5C, table S19) across trait definitions (fig. S23 to S24), supporting a shared physiological response to inhalational exposure. Several shared proteins have prior biological and genetic support linking them to smoking-related or neurobehavioral processes. Shared proteins included lung-enriched secretory proteins (SCGB1A1, SCGB3A1/SCGB3A2, SFTPA2) with established roles in airway epithelial function and known alteration by cigarette smoke (25, 26). NCAM1 was also strongly associated with both exposures (table S4); rs7935745 in NCAM1 is a well-replicated locus for smoking initiation, nicotine dependence, and smoking motives (27–29), and NCAM1 has an established role in synaptic plasticity (30–32). Additional shared proteins enriched in liver, gastrointestinal, and central nervous system (CNS) tissues included metabolic and neuroendocrine regulators (GHRL, POMC, IGFBP1, IGFBP2) (table S17 to S18), suggesting a neuroendocrine axis linking central appetite regulation with peripheral metabolic signaling (33, 34), consistent with prior experimental evidence (35–37). We note that tissue enrichment does not necessarily correspond to the tissues most highly represented or most abundantly measured on the Olink panel itself (Supplementary text). A subset of shared proteins showed opposing directions of effect between marijuana use and cigarette smoking, most notably the nitric oxide synthase NOS3 (eNOS), which was inversely associated with marijuana use but positively associated with current cigarette smoking (table S18, fig. S25, Supplementary text), consistent with distinct, well-characterized effects of cigarette smoke versus cannabinoids on nitric oxide signaling pathways (38–42). Proteins significant only for cigarette smoking (n=495) were enriched for pathways related to lung injury, extracellular matrix remodeling, and inflammation, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMP1, MMP8, MMP9, MMP12), vascular and endothelial markers (ICAM1, VEGFA), and surfactant-related proteins (SFTPD), consistent with established smoking-related pulmonary pathology (43–45). CHI3L1 (YKL-40), a wellestablished biomarker of inflammation and tissue remodeling, elevated in smokers and associated with chronic lung disease (46, 47) was also among these (table S18). Indeed these cigarette smoking proteins are highly enriched in the lung tissue (-log10FDR = 12.65, OR = 5.20) (Fig. 5C), consistent across alternative trait definitions (table S19, fig. S23 to S24). Fewer proteins were uniquely associated with marijuana use (n=187) than with cigarette smoking, despite comparable statistical power in this analysis, suggesting a narrower proteomic signature for marijuana use rather than a detection-power limitation. These proteins were most enriched in liver, connective/bone and immune/hematopoietic tissues, with a small subset (including CA14, previously implicated in schizophrenia (48)) also enriched in CNS regions (Fig. 5C, table S19). Among marijuana-specific proteins, NOS1 (nNOS) showed a pattern consistent with direct cannabinoid biology, given the established role of CB1 receptor activation in modulating nNOS-dependent nitric oxide signaling (49, 50) (Supplement text).

## Discussion

Plasma proteins could provide an objective molecular record of environmental exposure, but their value depends on three properties: consistency across populations, specificity across exposures, and reproducibility across cohorts. We tested all three in 9,561 All of Us participants profiled for 108 environmental, behavioral, socioeconomic, anthropometric, and clinical exposures. Associations were largely shared across ancestry and race and/or ethnicity strata, protein scores retained specificity across major exposure classes, and scores trained in UK Biobank transferred to All of Us for biologically proximal exposures. Yet score performance was not uniformly portable–evaluating generalizability requires joint consideration of biological consistency alongside exposure prevalence, social context, and cohort structure. Fewer than 1% of proteins per exposure showed significant heterogeneity across race and/or ethnicity and ancestry groups, suggesting that many proteomic responses to environmental and behavioral exposures are broadly shared. Yet, portability still requires calibration across race and/or ethnicity, sex, age, and social context, echoing lessons from polygenic scores (52, 53). BMI was the clearest exception, showing the greatest heterogeneity of any exposure tested. Leptin was most heterogeneous across ancestries, with trajectories diverging nonlinearly across ancestry, race and/or ethnicity, and sex, and sensitive to how BMI was scaled. Type 2 diabetes analyses reinforced the pattern: BMI-associated diabetes risk differed across ancestry and race and/or ethnicity, whereas leptin’s association was largely BMI-dependent, with residual sex-specific effect. We interpret BMI-linked proteomic signals as indexing socially and biologically patterned metabolic context rather than adiposity alone. We stress that race and/or ethnicity is not interchangeable with ancestry and that both are useful: ancestry is a continuum that approximates population genomic structure, whereas selfidentified race and/or ethnicity captures social and structural processes that genetics does not. An important caveat for our many cross-ancestry comparisons is Jensen's fallacy: the mistaken inference that because a trait is heritable within a population, differences in that trait between populations must also be genetic (54). Our own estimates illustrate why this distinction matters: SNP-heritability for height ranged from h2 = 0.395 in the AMR-like group to h2 = 0.602 in the EAS-like group, yet this within-population heritability does not indicate that the corresponding between-population difference in height, or in the protein signatures we study here, have a genetic versus environmental or cultural basis (55). The same caution applies to our broader cross-ancestry and cross-race and/or -ethnicity comparisons of exposure-protein associations. At the individual-protein level, many exposures shared associated proteins, consistent with pleiotropic inflammatory, metabolic, renal, hematologic, and airway responses. At the aggregated level, however, protein scores were largely exposure-specific across anthropometry, blood pressure, lipid, liver, and kidney domains. Specificity broke down where exposures are themselves entangled: tobacco and substance-use largely crosspredicted one another, reflecting real co-use patterns and shared inhalational biology. The PM2.5 score captured within-region variation and outperformed related environmental and geographic scores, yet also correlated with urbanization, socioeconomic status, inflammation, and smoking–reflecting challenges ahead for disentangling effects of pollution, deprivation, healthcare access, and comorbid disease risk that characterize environmental health disparities. Cross-biobank transfer was strong for exposures with direct, repeated physiological effects. UKB-trained scores for current smoking and alcohol use transferred cleanly to AoU across genetic ancestry groups, suggesting that reproducible biological responses extend beyond the cohort in which they were developed. Airpollution scores showed more limited transferability, likely reflecting cohort differences in geography, spatial resolution, and exposure modeling rather than a fundamental biological limit. These results highlight a distinctive contribution of AoU: its diversity across genetic ancestry, self-identified race and/or ethnicity,

AoU therefore provides a complementary setting for distinguishing shared biological response from context-specific exposure histories. Several limitations apply. Most analyses were cross-sectional, limiting temporal and causal inference. Protein signatures may reflect exposure effects, correlated exposures, compensatory physiology, subclinical disease, treatment, or reverse causation. Calibrating them to the social, epidemiologic, and biobank contexts in which they are applied will be essential to using them responsibly–such as disentangling how much of an observed disparity reflects differential exposure burden versus differential access to care– rather than reproducing existing measurement inequities. In conclusion, plasma proteomic signatures capture a broad range of environmental and behavioral exposures with generally limited cross-group heterogeneity, substantial exposure class specificity, and transferability for strong and biologically proximal exposure signatures. These findings establish proteomic exposure scores as a promising tool for exposure measurement, biobank harmonization, and health disparities research, while underscoring that their responsible use will require careful calibration and causal framework moving forward.

## Methods

## All of Us Data

The All of Us Research Program (AoU), launched by National Institute Health in May 2018, represents a longitudinal cohort study with the goal of engaging at least 1 million participants encompassing diverse ancestral backgrounds. By leveraging comprehensive data collection including biospecimens, health questionnaires, electronic health records and physical measurements, AoU aims to advance precision medicine and enhance overall human health (57). Participants, aged 18 years and older, are recruited from over 340 centers with informed consent. As of February 2025, a subset of around 414,830 participants has undergone whole genome sequencing (WGS). We used AoU plasma proteomics for this study. The AoU proteomics cohort measured 5,416 proteins across 10,170 individuals who were selected to maximize ancestral diversity using the Olink Explore 5K platform (AoU CDEv9, 2026). The proteomic data were released in version 9 and were paired with genetic and phenotypic data from version 8 for the present analyses(59). We used All of Us (AoU)-provided genetic ancestry classifications, which are based on principal components (PCs) computed from WGS data and describe genetic similarity to reference populations from the 1000 Genomes Project and Human Genome Diversity Project (1KGP-HGDP)(58). We refer to these groups as African (AFR-like), Americas (AMR-like), East Asian (EAS-like), European (EUR-like), Middle Eastern (MID-like), and South Asian (SAS-like); individuals not classified into one of these six groups, or reflecting admixture, are designated as remaining (REM) by AoU. Our sample included 1,865 AFR-like, 2,034 AMR-like, 1,382 SAS-like, 1,308 EAS-like, 2,999 EUR-like and 406 MID-like individuals. Self-identified race and/or ethnicity was assessed using AoU's "Race: What Race Ethnicity" survey variable (concept ID 1586140), a multi-select item from AoU's Basics survey with response options Asian, Black, Hispanic, MENA (Middle Eastern or North African), NHPI (Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander), White, and "None of these." Participants selecting exactly one of White, Black, Asian, or Hispanic were assigned to that category; participants selecting MENA, NHPI, or "None of these" (alone or in combination) were grouped as Other; and participants selecting more than one race and/or ethnicity category were classified as Mixed. Consequently, our Hispanic category reflects only participants who identified as Hispanic without concurrently selecting an additional race and/or ethnicity category; participants identifying as Hispanic in combination with another category were classified as Mixed. ## Preprocessing exposure data

We evaluated a broad set of health-related exposures and traits encompassing behavioral, socioeconomic, environmental, anthropometric, clinical, and biomarker domains. This exposure framework reflects domains commonly evaluated in prior social and environmental determinants of health and exposomic studies (1), expanded to incorporate additional environmental variables available through AoU's geocoded residential data (air pollution, ambient temperature, and neighborhood-level socioeconomic indices). The socioeconomic measures, including the deprivation index, education, income, were obtained from the socioeconomic status data available within the Controlled Tier dataset, which are externally sourced from the U.S. Census American Community Survey. For brevity, these variables are collectively referred to as “exposures” throughout the manuscript, although several traits, including anthropometric measures and clinical biomarkers, are influenced by both environmental and genetic factors. The final set comprised 108 exposure variables spanning tobacco and substance use (n=50, representing 15 distinct tobacco, alcohol, and substance-use constructs), anthropometry (n=3), blood pressure (n=2), socioeconomic characteristics (n=4), ambient temperature (n=4), air pollution (n =8, representing 6 distinct pollutants), hematologic biomarkers (n=18), glycemic biomarkers (n=3), lipid biomarkers (n=4), liver biomarkers (n=6), lung (n=1), thyroid (n=3), and kidney biomarkers (n=2) (table S2). The number of exposure variables exceeds the number of underlying exposure constructs because several domains were represented by multiple related measures, including lifetime-use, current-use, and exclusive-use tobacco and substance phenotypes, as well as short-term (30-day) and long-term (365-day) environmental exposure averages. Exposure variables were assembled from multiple AoU data resources. Tobacco, alcohol, and recreational drug use phenotypes were derived from responses to the Lifestyle survey and included lifetime (“ever”), current-use, and exclusive-use measures. Anthropometric traits, blood pressure measurements, and clinical biomarkers were obtained from the All of Us electronic health record (EHR) and Labs & Measurements data resources. Selection of clinical and biomarker traits was informed by the exposure framework used by Carrasco-Zanini et al.(1) for proteome-wide association analyses and corresponding variables were identified and curated from available All of Us survey, measurement, and EHR resources. Socioeconomic and contextual measures were derived from geocoded neighborhood-level datasets linked to participants’ residential locations. Binary exposures were analyzed as indicator variables. Continuous exposures were screened for extreme values, with observations exceeding 6 median absolute deviations from the median excluded prior to analysis and were subsequently inverse rank-normal transformed (IRNT). Sample size varied across exposures according to data availability, and analyses were conducted using all non-missing observations for each exposure. ## Individual Exposure-protein association analyses

We first evaluated associations between environmental exposures and individual plasma proteins to characterize exposure-related proteomic signals and assess their consistency across population groups. For each exposure, we performed univariate linear regression analyses in which each normalized plasma protein level (P) was regressed on the exposure of interest (E) and a set of covariates (C): 𝑃! = 𝛽# + 𝛽$𝐸! + 𝛾%𝐶! + 𝜖!. All models were adjusted for age at blood collection, sex, calendar year, month, and time of blood draw, based on prior evidence that these factors influence protein expression variability. For exposures derived from geocoded data, we additionally adjusted for geographic region (NorthEast/MidWest/Western/Southern) based on state of residence to account for broad spatial variation. Analyses were conducted both in the full pooled sample and within strata defined by population groups.

To assess consistency across groups, we compared exposure-protein regression coefficients (𝛽$) from groupstratified models using heterogeneity tests. Fixed-effects meta-analysis was performed across the group strata. Meta-analysis was conducted only for exposure-protein associations with valid regression estimates in at least two group strata. Associations were classified as heterogeneous if they were significant in the fixed-effects meta-analysis (Bonferroni-corrected p-value <0.05) and exhibited significant between-group heterogeneity according to Cochran’s Q test (p-value < 1.66 × 10⁻⁵, corresponding to 0.05 divided by 3,011 estimated independent proteins). The number of independent proteins was estimated using maximal independent set pruning of a protein correlation graph, where proteins were connected if their pairwise correlation exceeded r2 = 0.1.

## Cross score-exposure correlations

To evaluate cross-exposure prediction and exposure specificity, each exposure-trained protein score was assessed against all exposure targets in the held-out test set. For binary exposure targets, we calculated the point-biserial correlation between the continuous protein score and the 0/1-coded exposure indicator. This is equivalent to the Pearson correlation between a continuous variable and a binary variable coded as 0 and 1. For continuous exposure targets, we calculated the Pearson correlation between the protein score and the continuous exposure value. For all score-target pairs, we report both the signed correlation coefficient, r, and the squared correlation, R2, to summarize directionality and magnitude, respectively. Pairwise correlations were computed using complete observations for the corresponding score-target pair. To quantify exposure specificity, we compared the matched, diagonal score-exposure R2 with the maximum off-diagonal R2 across all non-matched exposure targets. Scores were classified as “on-target” if the matched exposure had a higher R2 than all off-diagonal targets. Scores for which an off-diagonal target exceeded the matched exposure were classified as “within-class” if the strongest off-diagonal target belonged to the same exposure class, or “between-class” if the strongest off-diagonal target belonged to a different exposure class. For phenotypic exposure-exposure correlations, binary-binary pairs were evaluated as Pearson correlations between two 0/1-coded variables, equivalent to the phi coefficient; binary-continuous pairs were evaluated using point-biserial correlations; and continuous-continuous pairs were evaluated using Pearson correlations. As a sensitivity analysis, we modeled off-diagonal score-exposure R2 as a function of phenotypic exposureexposure R2 across all off-diagonal pairs. Residual cross-prediction was defined as the observed off-diagonal score-exposure R2 minus the value expected from phenotypic R2. We then compared each score’s matched, diagonal R2 with its maximum residual off-diagonal cross-prediction to assess whether exposure specificity persisted after accounting for phenotypic correlation among exposures.

## Evaluation of UK Biobank-trained protein-exposure scores in All of Us

We evaluated the transferability of UK Biobank-trained protein-exposure scores in the All of Us Research Program. We focused on externally trained LASSO-based protein scores for current smoking and current alcohol drinking. For each exposure, external UKB score weights and model intercepts were applied to normalized AoU proteomic measurements using proteins that overlapped between the UKB score model and the AoU proteomic platform. The protein-exposure score for each participant was calculated as the sum of the model intercept and the weighted protein abundances, using the published UKB LASSO coefficient for each overlapping protein(7). AoU exposure phenotypes were harmonized to the corresponding UKB exposure definitions. Current smoking was evaluated using the binary AoU current smoking phenotype. Current alcohol drinking was defined using AoU alcohol questionnaire data, where users were participants who reported lifetime alcohol participation and non-never drinking in the past year, and non-users were participants who reported no lifetime alcohol participation. Participants with missing or ambiguous alcohol-drinking status were excluded from the corresponding analysis. Score performance was evaluated in the full proteomics AoU analysis set and stratified by genetically inferred ancestry. Analyses were performed separately in EUR-like, AMR-like, AFR-like, EAS-like, and SAS-like groups. For each exposure and ancestry group, discrimination was quantified using the AUCs, with 95% confidence intervals estimated using DeLong’s method. AUCs were calculated using the external UKB proteinexposure score as the predictor and the harmonized AoU exposure phenotype as the binary outcome, adjusting for age, sex, collection year, month of sample collection, and time of day of sample collection. Full descriptions of the prevalence-matched sensitivity analysis are provided in the Materials and Methods.

## Tissue enrichment for Proteomic signatures of behavioral exposures

We performed GTEx-based tissue enrichment analysis using GTEx v10 median gene expression values. The GTEx v10 gene median TPM matrix was read into R and converted to a SummarizedExperiment object with genes as rows and tissues as columns. Gene symbols from the GTEx Description column were used to match Olink protein identifiers. Rows with missing or invalid gene identifiers were removed, and duplicate gene symbols were collapsed by retaining the maximum median TPM across duplicate rows for each tissue. Tissue-elevated gene sets were defined using the teGeneRetrieval() function from the TissueEnrich R package(60), which applies a Human Protein Atlas-style tissue-specificity classification to expression matrices. We used a four-fold expression threshold, a maximum of five tissues for group-enriched genes, and a minimum expression threshold of 1 TPM. Genes classified as Tissue-Enriched, Group-Enriched, or Tissue- Enhanced were considered tissue-elevated. Non-tissue-elevated categories, including Expressed-In-All, Mixed, and Not-Expressed, were not used as tissue-specific sets. For each pair of traits, proteins were classified into four mutually exclusive groups: associated with both traits, associated with the first trait only, associated with the second trait only, or associated with neither trait. Gene symbols from the Olink protein panel were matched to the GTEx/TissueEnrich reference gene set, and proteins without a matching GTEx annotation were excluded. For each tissue, we compared each target group (Both, trait 1 only, and trait 2 only) against the Neither group – comprising all remaining Olink panel proteins not significantly associated with either trait – using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests. ## GWAS validation for Proteomic signatures of behavioral exposures

To provide genetic context for the proteomic findings, we examined publicly available genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for cigarette smoking initiation and lifetime cannabis use. Summary statistics for smoking initiation were obtained from the GWAS meta-analysis reported by Saunders et al. (2022)(27), comprising individuals of European ancestry (n = 2,669,029). Summary statistics for lifetime cannabis use were obtained from the Bright et al. (2026)(51) European-ancestry GWAS (total effective sample size: 258,823). Only variants present in both datasets were retained for downstream comparisons. To facilitate comparison between traits, effect estimates were harmonized to the same effect allele, and genome-wide significant loci were annotated to the nearest protein-coding gene using standard genomic annotation. To characterize the tissues and cell types implicated by genetic susceptibility to smoking initiation and lifetime cannabis use, we performed gene-property and cell-type enrichment analyses using FUMA v1.6.x (Functional Mapping and Annotation of GWAS(61)). Independent genome-wide significant variants (P < 5 × 10⁻⁸) were mapped to genes using the default FUMA SNP2GENE pipeline. Tissue-specific expression enrichment was evaluated using GTEx (v8), and cell-type specificity analyses were performed using the precomputed singlecell RNA sequencing reference datasets implemented in FUMA (including Tabula Muris FACS). Enrichment significance was assessed using the default MAGMA gene-property framework implemented in FUMA, and tissues or cell types with FDR-adjusted P < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

## SNP-heritability estimation

We estimated SNP-heritability (h2) for 108 exposure and biomarker traits across five ancestry groups in the All of Us v8 cohort (AFR-like N=74,575; AMR-like N=70,626; EAS-like N=9,706; EUR-like N=75,000; SAS-like N=5,368) using GCTA-GREML(62) (v1.94.1) with ancestry-stratified genomic relationship matrices built from unrelated individuals. All models adjusted for age, age2, sex, and 16 genetic PCs. Significance of each h2 estimate was assessed via GCTA's likelihood-ratio test and corrected for multiple testing (540 tests) using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. Estimates falling outside the valid (0,1) range were excluded from summary statistics.
